title: CIA Informant Who Infiltrated al-Qaeda for a Decade Detained by ICE, Faces Deportation
excerpt: Blerim Skoro risked his life infiltrating terrorist networks after 9/11 — now the father of three US citizens sits in a New Jersey detention facility.
body:
• Blerim Skoro, 55, a former CIA informant who infiltrated al-Qaeda for nearly a decade, was detained by ICE on August 3 during a routine biometrics appointment in New Jersey
  • The Kosovan refugee provided intelligence on terrorist plots, weapons shipments, and al-Qaeda operations across Pakistan, the Middle East, and the Balkans after being recruited the day after 9/11
  • Skoro was granted leave to remain in 2022 under the UN Convention against Torture, but was arrested while renewing his work permit under the current immigration enforcement push
  • His lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition seeking immediate release, arguing the US government failed to honor promises of lawful residency

Blerim Skoro spent nearly a decade risking his life as a CIA informant, infiltrating al-Qaeda camps in Pakistan and intercepting terrorist plots across the Middle East. On August 3, the 55-year-old father of three was handcuffed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at a New Jersey office where he had gone to renew his work permit.

Skoro, a Kosovan refugee who fled to the United States in 1994 after deserting the Yugoslav Army, is now being held at an ICE detention facility in Elizabeth, New Jersey, and faces potential deportation — despite years of service to US national security and previous legal protections against removal.

From Prison Cell to al-Qaeda Camps

Skoro's path into espionage began the day after the September 11, 2001 attacks. Serving a seven-year sentence for drug trafficking at a federal prison in Pennsylvania, he was recruited by CIA agents who saw his background as a Kosovar Muslim — with military experience and deep Quranic knowledge — as ideal for infiltrating jihadist networks, according to The Times of London.

While still incarcerated, he began sharing information with the FBI and CIA on his cellmates, including Mokhtar Haouari, an Algerian behind the so-called Millennium Plot to bomb Los Angeles International Airport.

"I didn't give it a second's thought. I considered myself a patriot of America first and a Muslim second. I wanted to pay back this country."

— Blerim Skoro, speaking to The Times in November 2024

After his deportation to Kosovo in 2007, Skoro's work intensified. He infiltrated al-Qaeda camps in Pakistan during the hunt for Osama bin Laden, intercepted ISIS terror plots in Syria, and operated across Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, and the Balkans. He gained the trust of senior al-Qaeda leaders who tasked him with procuring anti-aircraft missiles, stingers, and rocket launchers for jihadists in the Balkans — shipments the CIA intercepted based on his intelligence.

Skoro also claims he helped intercept shipments of uranium to Kosovo, preventing a possible dirty bomb plot.

Abandoned After a Decade of Service

His covert career ended abruptly in 2010 when he was ambushed and shot while traveling to a CIA safe house in Macedonia. Rather than being evacuated to safety in the US, he was given a cash payment in an envelope and told to cross back into Kosovo, according to his account.

Tired of waiting for the green card he says the CIA had promised, Skoro traveled through Canada and crossed into the US in 2015 to rejoin his wife Susan and their three children — all US citizens. He was arrested after using his daughter's Metro card on the subway and spent six months in federal detention.

After a six-year legal battle, Skoro was granted leave to remain in 2022 under the United Nations Convention against Torture, after demonstrating that returning to Kosovo could result in torture or death due to his undercover work. The ruling prevents deportation to Kosovo but allows removal to a willing third country.

Detained Amid Enforcement Surge

Skoro's August 3 arrest came as ICE officers operate under pressure to meet daily arrest targets reported to be between 2,000 and 3,000 per day. Arrests by local law enforcement partnering with ICE have surged to an average of 3,000 per month in early 2026, compared to 250 per month in 2024 under President Biden, according to data from the University of California Berkeley's Deportation Data Project.

"I'm telling the officer, 'Google my name and see who I am, I am a public person.' He said, 'I see who you are but I'm sorry I just have to do my job.' I heard one supervisor tell other agents: 'I don't see how the president would want to put in prison someone who has served our nation for a decade.'"

— Blerim Skoro, to The Times

In a filing to the New Jersey district court on August 17, Skoro wrote that he works up to 70 hours per week as a taxi driver to support his family and has not committed any crimes since the 2022 ruling. His lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition seeking his immediate release.

What's Next

The case has drawn attention from immigration advocates and national security observers alike. Skoro's story was the subject of a 2024 documentary, The Accidental Spy, and his claims are supported by video footage he recorded undercover and correspondence with handlers.

His pro-bono lawyer, Renee Kathawala, said Skoro "is the face of why immigration is a positive force in our country — he is patriotic, he sacrificed his life for ours, and he dedicated himself to the most challenging job possible."

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not respond to requests for comment. For the broader immigrant community — including those who have served US interests abroad — the case raises unsettling questions about whether promises made in the shadows of national security will be honored in the daylight of enforcement crackdowns.

nri_angle: Immigration enforcement affecting even those who served US national security — raises concerns in diaspora communities about deportation policies and broken government promises.
